tip: The command form is just the verb stem: 'rijden' drops '-en' to give 'rijd'.
'Stoppen' and 'beginnen' take 'met' before the activity: 'stop met klagen', 'begin met werken'.
To compare, adjectives add '-er' and use 'dan' for than: 'kouder dan de herfst'.
'Haasten' needs 'je' pointing back at the subject: 'haast je niet' means don't rush.
'Opgeven' splits: the prefix 'op' breaks off and moves to the end, giving 'geef ... op'.
'Gaan' plus an infinitive marks the near future: 'het gaat regenen' means it is going to rain.
A 'de' word like 'kaas' is referred to as 'hij', not 'het', even for a thing: 'hij is echt heerlijk'.
'Als' (if/when) pushes the verb of its clause to the end: 'als je moe bent'.
'Elk' means each and takes a singular noun: 'elk kleinkind', not 'elk kleinkinderen'.
A noun ending in '-ing' makes its little form with '-etje': 'wandeling' becomes 'wandelingetje'.
'Het' words use 'dat' to attach a description, 'de' words use 'die': 'het kind dat huilt'.
Even long adjectives usually just add '-er' instead of a word for more: 'interessanter', not 'meer interessant'.
'Want' means because but keeps normal word order, verb in second place: 'want het waait hard'.
'Zijn' has an irregular command form, 'wees', so 'wees niet bang' means don't be afraid.
Dutch uses the present tense for the future when a time word is there: 'gaat volgend jaar'.
After a quantity word the noun follows directly, with no 'van': 'een slokje water'.
Units of measure like 'jaar' usually stay singular after a number: 'honderd jaar', not 'honderd jaren'.
After 'gewend' (used to), the activity follows with 'om ... te' plus a verb: 'om vroeg te eten'.
Dutch often uses 'zitten' for where a shop or business is located: 'de winkel die op de hoek zit'.
'Ervan' fuses 'er' and 'van' to mean of it: 'wat je ervan vindt' means what you think of it.
'Er' fills the subject slot when the real subject is indefinite, like 'een bus': 'er rijdt een bus'.
Drop the article before a profession after 'als': 'werkt als arts', not 'als een arts'.
'Gaan over' is the usual way to say to be about: 'gaat over het leven in Amsterdam'.
When something is done to the subject, 'door' marks who does it: 'door het parlement' means by parliament.
'Worden' plus a past participle says what is being done to the subject: 'wordt ... gefinancierd' means is being funded.
'Wier' is a formal word for whose, used for a woman or a group: 'de vrouw wier dochter ziek is'.
'Enerzijds' pairs with 'anderzijds' (on one hand ... on the other) and puts the verb before the subject: 'enerzijds vind ik'.
To say what something is made of, use 'van' plus the material: 'oorbelletjes van zilver' = earrings made of silver.
Every diminutive ('-je' word) is a 'het' word, so the adjective after 'een' gets no '-e': 'een rood jurkje', not 'rode'.
'Zullen' builds the future and sends the main verb to the end as an infinitive: 'zal in maart opengaan'.
